title: Benjamin Franklin and the Lightning Rod: Science as the Common Heritage of Humanity
summary: After inventing the revolutionary lightning rod in 1752, Benjamin Franklin steadfastly refused to patent the device, insisting that scientific inventions must freely serve human safety.
full_text:
In the summer of 1752, in Philadelphia, Benjamin Franklin conducted his celebrated kite experiment, demonstrating that atmospheric lightning and terrestrial electricity were identical physical phenomena.

Applying this breakthrough, Franklin designed the lightning rod—an iron rod affixed to rooftops connected to a ground wire, quietly channeling destructive electrical charges safely into the earth. The invention instantly revolutionized public safety across Europe and America, preventing catastrophic fires that had plagued cities for centuries.

Entrepreneurs and close associates urged Franklin to secure an exclusive royal patent immediately:
"Dr. Franklin, you can secure exclusive patent rights across Britain and the American colonies! Every church, port, warehouse, and estate must purchase this rod. You will amass a colossal fortune!"

Franklin declined the lucrative proposal without a moment's hesitation, articulating a principle of open science that astonished his contemporaries:
"That, as we enjoy great advantages from the inventions of others, we should be glad of an opportunity to serve others by any invention of ours; and this we should do freely and generously!
Can a man legitimately monopolize the fire of heaven? If Providence permits us to understand a law of nature to shield our neighbor's home from fire, to charge a tax upon his safety would be unconscionable. Science is not a private preserve of commerce; it is the common inheritance of mankind!"

Refusing all royalties, Franklin published detailed instructions in Poor Richard's Almanack so any blacksmith could construct the rod freely. His generosity established the modern ethos of open scientific inquiry for public welfare.
